subject: math

unit.title: Calculation: add, subtract, multiply, divide
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we add and take away bigger numbers, and what does 'lots of' mean?

title: Multiplication: equal groups and arrays
objectives: By the end, I can show a multiplication as equal groups and as an array.

vocabulary.definition: groups with exactly the same number in each
dots arranged in neat rows and columns
count equal groups the fast way

emphasize: Multiplication is EQUAL GROUPS — '3 × 5' means 3 groups of 5, counted the fast way (skip-counting!).
Turn an array a quarter-turn and the dots don't change: 3 × 5 = 5 × 3. Pre-empt '3 × 5 and 5 × 3 are different sums.'
Pre-empt the + / × mix-up: 3 × 5 is NOT 3 + 5. Repeat: 'Same dots, same total — turn it and check.'

misconceptions: thinking 3 × 5 and 5 × 3 are different sums needing separate work
hooks: 4 plates, 5 grapes on each — how many grapes without counting them all?

digital: virtual counters and dot arrays on the whiteboard block (animated rotation)

video.watchTask: Every time the blocks line up in rows and columns, freeze! Say the two facts the array shows (like 3 × 5 and 5 × 3).

afterCheck.question: When the blocks turned their rectangle sideways, did the number of blocks change?
afterCheck.expectedAnswer: No — same blocks, same total, just turned.

plan.goal: Pose the lazy-genius problem: 4 plates of 5 grapes — count them WITHOUT counting them all; retrieve skip-counting.
plan.note: Let the child discover that skip-counting in 5s solves it — that's the bridge from Lesson 5.

script.say: Look at this feast! Four plates, and on every plate — five grapes. I want to know how many grapes altogether… but I am FAR too lazy to count them one by one. You know a super-speed trick from last time, don't you? Count the plates with me: 5… 10… keep going!
script.adaptHints: Swap grapes for a snack the child loves. Listen for 15, 20; if shaky, skip-count one plate at a time together.

stuckProtocol: If skip-counting is shaky: point at one plate at a time and chant together — 5… 10… 15… 20.

plan.goal: Name the × sign as 'groups of', line the groups into an array, rotate it a quarter-turn and prove 3 × 5 = 5 × 3.
plan.note: The rotation is the heart of the lesson — same dots, same total. Show both counts: 5, 10, 15 and 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees the 3×5 array turn into 5×3 with the same 15 dots and hears 'same dots, same total'.

script.say: Here's the magic sign: ×. It means 'groups of'. Three groups of 5 counters is 'three times five' — written 3 × 5. Now watch me tidy the groups into neat rows: 3 rows, 5 in each row. That's called an ARRAY. Count the rows in fives: 5, 10, 15 — fifteen! Now the magic trick… I turn the whole array a quarter-turn. Look! Now it's 5 rows of 3. But did any dot appear or disappear? Not one! Same dots, same total — so 3 × 5 equals 5 × 3. Every array gives you TWO facts for the price of one.
script.adaptHints: Make the rotation playful — 'ta-da!'. Repeat the anchor: 'Same dots, same total — turn it and check.'

plan.goal: Shared build of 2 × 5: child names groups and group-size, totals it, and predicts the turned fact.
plan.note: The child directs: how many groups, how many in each, what happens on the turn. 2 × 5 = 10 = 5 × 2.
plan.successCriteria: Child builds/reads 2 groups of 5, answers 10, and says 5 × 2 is also 10 without recounting.

script.say: Your turn to be the array chef! Show me 2 × 5. How many groups? … How many in each group? … Now line them into an array — 2 rows of 5. Count it the fast way… ten! Now the big prediction, no counting allowed: if we turn it into 5 rows of 2, how many dots will there be?
script.adaptHints: If the child wants to recount after the turn, let them once — then ask 'did any dot escape?'

check.question: 2 × 5 = ? And what is 5 × 2?
check.expectedAnswer: 10 — and 5 × 2 is also 10, same dots turned

wrongAnswers.remedy: × means GROUPS OF. Make 2 groups of 5 and count them in fives: 5, 10.

wrongAnswers.why: multiplied 5 × 5 — lost track of the number of groups
wrongAnswers.remedy: How many GROUPS are there? Count the rows first, then the dots in one row.

plan.goal: Diagnostic: 3 × 5, plus the commutativity probe — if 2 × 10 = 20, what is 10 × 2 without recounting?
plan.note: The two KB traps: '8' means × read as +; recalculating 10 × 2 means commutativity hasn't landed.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 15, then answers 20 for 10 × 2 instantly, citing the turn.

script.say: Quiz time! First: 3 × 5 — think groups, count fast. … Now the detective part: I'll tell you that 2 × 10 = 20. Without building anything, without counting — what is 10 × 2? And HOW do you know?
script.adaptHints: After correct answers, probe: 'How do you know 10 × 2 without recounting?' Listen for 'turn the array / same dots'.

blocks.explain: 3 groups of 5: count in fives — 5, 10, 15. (Not 3 + 5 = 8 — the × sign means groups of!)

check.question: 3 × 5 = ? And if 2 × 10 = 20, what is 10 × 2?
check.expectedAnswer: 15; and 20 — turning the array keeps the same dots

wrongAnswers.remedy: × means groups of. Build 3 groups of 5 — now count them in fives.
Picture the 2 × 10 array and turn it a quarter-turn. Did any dot appear or vanish? So the total is…?

plan.goal: Independent building and reading of equal groups and arrays, writing BOTH facts each time; stretch to 5 × 5 and spotting non-equal groups.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. Insist on both commutative facts where the item asks.
plan.successCriteria: Child completes 3+ items including one array-reading item and one both-facts item.

script.say: Array-chef practice! I'll serve you plates, rows and dots. Your jobs: check the groups are EQUAL, count the fast way, and — chef's bonus — serve every array with its two matching facts.
script.adaptHints: Swap grapes/dots for the child's favourite small things (never change the numbers). Celebrate skip-counted totals.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'the groups weren't equal' or '× got read as +.'
Go concrete — build the equal groups as separate plates on the board before any array.
One hint: 'How many groups? How many in each?'
Re-ask with 2 groups of 2, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states what × means and why 3 × 5 = 5 × 3; end on an earned success.
plan.successCriteria: Child says × means 'groups of' and explains the turn keeps the same dots.

script.say: Two last chef questions! What does the × sign tell us to do? … And why is 3 × 5 exactly the same as 5 × 3? … Yes — groups of, and turning the array keeps every single dot. You turned the array to PROVE the two facts match — you earned two facts for the price of one, every time. That trick will make the times tables twice as easy next lesson!
script.adaptHints: Praise the specific process observed: checking groups were equal, skip-counting instead of counting by ones, predicting before turning.

block.prompt: 2 plates with 5 grapes on each — how many grapes altogether?

wrongAnswers.remedy: That's the + move! Here we have GROUPS: point at each plate and count in fives — 5, then…?

wrongAnswers.why: counted 5 groups of 5 — lost the group count
wrongAnswers.remedy: How many plates are there? Touch each plate as you skip-count.

hints: Count in 5s, one plate per number: 5, …?
2 groups of 5 — the answer comes on the second five.

reteach.say: One plate — 5 grapes. Two plates — count on: 5… 10. Two groups of five make ten. Groups first, then skip-count — that's the whole trick.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Every group adds a full 2. What's 6 and 2 more?
There are only 4 groups — one number per group. 2, 4, 6… that's three groups… one more?

hints: One number for each group: 4 groups, 4 numbers.

reteach.say: March through the groups: group one — 2, group two — 4, group three — 6, group four — 8. Four groups of 2 make 8, and that's the fact 4 × 2 = 8!

wrongAnswers.remedy: × means groups of! Make 3 groups of 5 in your head and count them in fives.

wrongAnswers.why: wrote the two digits side by side
wrongAnswers.remedy: We're counting dots, not gluing digits. 3 groups of 5: 5, 10, …?

hints: 3 groups of 5 — count in fives, three numbers.

reteach.say: 3 × 5 says: three groups, five in each. Count the fast way — 5, 10, 15. Three fives are fifteen. If you ever catch yourself doing 3 + 5, remember: × means GROUPS OF.

wrongAnswers.remedy: × means groups of — 4 groups with 2 in each. Skip-count: 2, 4, 6, …?

wrongAnswers.why: wrote the digits side by side
wrongAnswers.remedy: Build it: 4 pairs of socks. Count in twos.

hints: 4 groups of 2 — one number per group.

reteach.say: Four pairs of socks: 2, 4, 6, 8. Four twos make eight — 4 × 2 = 8. The × just tells you how many equal jumps to make.

block.prompt: An array has 5 rows with 2 dots in each row. Which fact matches it?
block.explain: 5 rows of 2: count in twos — 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. The array shows 5 × 2 = 10.

wrongAnswers.why: read the array as an addition of the side lengths
wrongAnswers.remedy: The array is FULL of dots, not just two numbers. Count the dots in twos, row by row.

wrongAnswers.why: right fact shape, but total came from adding
wrongAnswers.remedy: Good — 5 rows of 2! Now count the actual dots: 2, 4, 6, 8, …?

hints: Count row by row in twos: 2, 4, 6…

reteach.say: Reading an array is a two-step dance: count the ROWS (5), count the dots IN one row (2), then skip-count the whole thing: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Five twos are ten.

block.explain: Turn the 3 × 5 array a quarter-turn: it becomes 5 × 3 — but not one dot appears or vanishes. Both are 15.

wrongAnswers.why: the lesson's core misconception — sees two different sums
wrongAnswers.remedy: Picture the 3 rows of 5 dots. Turn it. Count the dots again — did any escape?

wrongAnswers.why: thinks the first number decides the size
wrongAnswers.remedy: Same dots either way! Skip-count both: 5, 10, 15 and 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. What do you notice?

hints: Turn the array — do the dots change?
Count both ways: in fives (3 numbers) and in threes (5 numbers).

reteach.say: The turning trick never fails: 3 rows of 5, turn it, 5 rows of 3 — the same 15 dots just standing sideways. That's why every array hands you TWO facts: 3 × 5 = 15 and 5 × 3 = 15.

block.prompt: Match each fact to its total.

wrongAnswers.remedy: × means groups of. Skip-count 3 fives: 5, 10, 15. Which total is that?
TWO tens only — one number per group: 10, 20. Stop there!

hints: Skip-count each one — one number per group.
The 10s facts end in 0; count the tens jumps.

reteach.say: Every fact is a skip-count with a stop sign: 3 × 5 → 5, 10, 15, stop. 2 × 10 → 10, 20, stop. 4 × 2 → 2, 4, 6, 8, stop. 3 × 10 → 10, 20, 30, stop. Count the groups on your fingers so you stop in time!

block.prompt: Stretch! Picture a 5-by-5 array — 5 rows, 5 in each row. 5 × 5 = ?

wrongAnswers.remedy: That's the + move. Five ROWS of five — skip-count a whole hand per row: 5, 10, …
Five rows need five numbers. 5, 10, 15, 20 — that's only four rows. One more!

hints: Five rows = five numbers in your skip-count.

reteach.say: A 5 × 5 array is a perfect square of dots. Row by row: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Five fives are twenty-five — and here's a secret: turn it and it looks EXACTLY the same. Square arrays are their own twins!

block.prompt: Can you multiply it? Sort these!

items.text: a pile of 2 and a pile of 6

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: 3 plates of 5, 4 bags of 2, 5 rows of 3 → equal; plates with 2, 3 and 4, piles of 2 and 6 → not equal

wrongAnswers.answer: plates with 2, 3 and 4 grapes → can multiply
wrongAnswers.why: sees groups but doesn't check they're EQUAL
wrongAnswers.remedy: Multiplication needs every group the SAME. Are 2, 3 and 4 the same? Could you skip-count those plates?

wrongAnswers.answer: a pile of 2 and a pile of 6 → can multiply
wrongAnswers.why: two groups looks like ×, but the groups differ
wrongAnswers.remedy: Try skip-counting it — what step would you use? 2? 6? Neither fits both piles.

hints: One question decides: is every group EXACTLY the same size?
If you can't skip-count it with one step, you can't multiply it.

reteach.say: Multiplication is fussy: every group must match exactly, or the skip-count breaks. 3 plates of 5 — count 5, 10, 15, lovely. Plates of 2, 3 and 4 — what step would you even use? None fits! Unequal groups need adding, not multiplying.

block.prompt: Leo says 3 × 5 = 8. What did he do wrong, and what's the real answer?
block.sample: He added 3 + 5. But × means groups of — 3 groups of 5. Skip-count: 5, 10, 15. The real answer is 15.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: He added instead of making groups; 3 × 5 means 3 groups of 5, which is 15

wrongAnswers.remedy: Build 3 plates of 5 and count every grape. Do you get 8 — or a lot more?

wrongAnswers.why: swapped one error for the digit-gluing error
wrongAnswers.remedy: No gluing digits! Count the actual dots in 3 groups of 5: 5, 10, …?

hints: What does the × sign mean — join two numbers, or make groups?
Draw Leo's sum as 3 plates of 5 and count.

reteach.say: The two signs are different machines: + POOLS two piles (3 + 5 = 8), but × COPIES a group (3 copies of 5). Three plates of five grapes is way more than 8 — it's 5, 10, 15. Same digits, totally different jobs!

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → move up one level; at level 3, interleave array-reading, both-facts and equal/unequal sorting.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach with the equal groups built as separate plates first, then serve a level-1 item (2 groups of 2).
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one array item and one commutativity item (stating the turned fact without recounting) → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'multiplication as equal groups and arrays'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'the groups weren't equal' or '× got read as +.'
Go concrete — physically make the equal groups as plates before any array.
One hint: 'How many groups? How many in each?'
Re-ask with 2 groups of 2, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Make the groups out of LearnerModel.interests (grapes, football stickers, toy cars in rows) — never change the numbers or the groups-of language.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish with an item the child can win (2 groups of 2 if needed), then specific process praise: what they DID (checked the groups were equal, skip-counted, turned the array to prove two facts) — never 'you're so clever'.

differentiation.support: Count every array in skip-counts with one finger per row; keep the groups physically separated on plates until arrays feel safe.
differentiation.stretch: Write both facts for every array unaided; 'would turning ANY array always keep the same total? Why?'; build the 5 × 5 square and find its twin.

extension: 'Spin the array' — make an array, predict the turned fact, spin it and check; collect five matching pairs of facts.
assessmentEvidence: Child represents a multiplication as equal groups AND as an array, states the total by skip-counting, and writes both commutative facts.
revisitLater: Arrays return in Lesson 10 (the 2, 5 and 10 times tables) and Lesson 11 (division as sharing); the daily skip-count starter keeps the totals warm.
